query: Earlier studies on stainless, alloy, and boiler steels reported improved hardness, wear resistance, thermal stability, or reduced mass change during aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C. However, these findings were specific to individual material systems and emphasized characterization or performance rather than establishing why corrosion protection persists or fails across room- and high-temperature regimes; studies combining HEAs, subsequent annealing, and hot-corrosion assessment were also reported to be minimal. For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its corrosion-related degradation or retention of protection under these regimes? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to an appropriate reference, the conditions under which the hypothesis should and should not apply, supporting evidence from the earlier studies, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In unexposed Q235 steel, corrosion resistance at room temperature and moderate high temperatures (≈700 °C) derives from a thin, protective native oxide film whose integrity is maintained; however, when exposed to aggressive salt atmospheres (e.g., Na2SO4/NaCl mixtures) at higher temperatures (800–900 °C), salt‐assisted fluxing and thermal activation induce compositional and morphological degradation of the protective oxide, leading to accelerated corrosion.
generation.material_initial_state: Pre-exposure Q235 steel with its native oxide layer and unmodified microstructure.
generation.intervention: Expose Q235 steel samples to a controlled salt mixture (e.g., 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl) under staged temperature conditions (room temperature, 700 °C, 800 °C, and 900 °C) while performing in situ high-temperature XRD and cross-sectional electron microscopy analysis.
generation.conditions: Experiments will be conducted under a fixed oxygen partial pressure (in air) and in the presence of the aggressive salt at each temperature stage. Reference tests include Q235 samples exposed in identical temperature regimes without salt and samples of a known corrosion-resistant steel (e.g., stainless steel) under identical salt exposure.
generation.structural_mediator: The evolution, integrity, and phase composition of the surface oxide scale on Q235 steel, as revealed by in situ XRD and electron microscopy.
generation.mechanism: At lower temperatures the native oxide on Q235 forms a coherent, protective barrier. However, at high temperatures under salt exposure, salt-driven fluxing leads to selective leaching and phase transformations within the oxide film, causing oxide thinning, spallation, or composition change that compromises the barrier and accelerates corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: At room temperature and near 700 °C, minimal corrosion will occur with stable oxide scales; at 800–900 °C, salt exposure will trigger degradation of the oxide film, evidenced by increased mass loss, breakdown or spallation of the oxide, and formation of non-protective corrosion products relative to baseline samples or the stainless steel reference.
generation.baseline: Q235 steel samples subjected to identical temperature profiles without salt exposure, and corrosion-resistant stainless steel tested under the same salt and temperature conditions.
generation.boundary: The mechanism is expected to apply only when both high temperatures and aggressive salt environments are present; in inert atmospheres or in the absence of salt, the native oxide should remain stable and protective.
generation.uncertainty: The detailed composition of the native oxide on Q235 and its exact transformation pathways under coupled thermal and salt stress are not fully established; additional factors such as minor alloying elements and microstructural heterogeneities may influence the protective behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare several sets of Q235 steel samples and subject them to controlled exposures in a fixed salt mixture (75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl) at room temperature, 700 °C, 800 °C, and 900 °C while monitoring the surface in situ via high-temperature XRD and by cross-sectional SEM/EDS. Include control samples with no salt exposure and a reference corrosion-resistant steel under identical conditions.
measurements: Mass change before and after exposure
XRD phase identification of the surface oxide at each temperature
SEM imaging and EDS for oxide morphology and composition
Assessment of oxide scale thickness and evidence of spallation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If high-temperature salt exposure (particularly at 800–900 °C) does not result in detectable degradation, compositional changes, or structural breakdown of the oxide scale (i.e., the oxide remains continuous and protective with no significant increase in mass loss or evidence of spallation compared to the controls), then the hypothesis that salt-driven oxide breakdown is the mechanism driving corrosion failure in Q235 steel will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Early research reported that stainless steel, Fe-Cr alloy, and CrFe15Ni15 alloy have excellent corrosion resistance due to the dense Cr2O3 passivation film formed on the surface [,,]. Similarly, it was speculated that the Cr2O3 passivation film has the same effect in the corrosion resistance of HEAs. AlCoCrFeNi [], AlxCrFe1.5MnNi0.5 [], and Al0.5CoCrCuFeNiBx [] verified the foregoing speculation. Therefore, for the (CoCrFeNi)95Nb5 HEA coating passivation film of this study, it can be obtained from the results of XPS that the Cr2O3 in the passivation film provides good corrosion resistance for the coating, and the addition of trace amount of Nb results in forming a stable metal oxide of Nb2O5 in the passivation film of the coating, which also plays a positive role in the corrosion resistance [,].

This study aims to test the effect of the elemental stability inherent in HEAs due to the high configurational entropy and/or sluggish diffusion (if any) on the elemental dissolution in the molten salt. Specifically, the study focuses on corrosion performance and thermal stability of the Cr18Mn27Fe27.5Ni27.5 alloy in molten fluoride salt environment. This multi-component alloy with both Mn and Cr which are reactive in molten fluoride salt is well suited to test these hypotheses. This high entropy alloy was exposed to molten FLiBe salt at 700 °C for 1000 hours followed by detailed analysis of corrosion in the near-surface regions of the alloy in terms of elemental dissolution into the molten salt and morphological changes at the surface. The results were compared to that of 316 H stainless steel tested under similar conditions.

decision.trend: Early work (PMC6908586, 2019) explored high-temperature molten salt corrosion of a CrMnFeNi-based high-entropy alloy at 700 °C, revealing that selective leaching of certain elements and secondary phase precipitation influence corrosion resistance. Subsequent experiments (PMC8200011, 2021) applied laser-deposited high-entropy coatings onto carbon steels, showing that, despite improved erosion–corrosion performance under moderately high-temperature geothermal conditions, defects in the coatings could still degrade their protective capabilities. More recent studies (PMC8875499, 2022) used post-annealing to transform high-entropy alloy coatings into mixed-phase microstructures with potentially enhanced corrosion resistance. Across these efforts, however, the focus remained on alloy- or coating-specific behavior, leaving the precise, fundamental mechanism of how steels—particularly low-carbon structural steels such as Q235—retain or lose their corrosion protection from room temperature up to 700–900 °C under aggressive salt environments still only partially understood.
decision.unsolved: It remains unclear whether Q235’s protective surface films and interfacial phases undergo specific morphological or compositional transitions at increasing temperatures that favor or diminish hot-corrosion resistance in salty atmospheres. The interplay among protective oxide stability, salt-driven fluxing processes, and alloy substrate transformations needs systematic study to pinpoint when and why corrosion failures initiate and whether certain postexposure treatments (e.g., annealing) can preserve barrier layers.
decision.lever: Perform staged in situ high-temperature XRD and cross-sectional electron microscopy to track oxide evolution on Q235 during salt exposure from room temperature to 900 °C under controlled salt and gas atmospheres.
decision.why: Directly observing the formation, growth, and breakdown of protective scales and corrosion products at successive temperatures and environments will identify the microstructural triggers responsible for the transition from stable to failing corrosion protection. By comparing surface morphologies, compositions, and phase transformations over a range of conditions and against a reference steel, researchers can test the hypothesis that the integrity and composition of the oxide scale determine Q235’s corrosion performance and clarify when oxide breakdown promotes salt-assisted degradation.
